```{r}
set.seed(100)
```

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean Difference (Two-Tailed)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 28.1"}
Let $(X_{i1}, X_{i2})$ for $i = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ be a sequence of independent pairs of normally distributed random variables, (i.e., $\text{Cov}[X_{i1}, X_{i2}] = \sigma_{12}$), with means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and standard deviations $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$. Let $D_i = X_{i1}-X_{i2}$ be independent differences for each pair with mean $\mu_d = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ and standard deviation $\sigma_d = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\sigma_{12}}$

When performing a hypothesis test to test $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ vs $H_A: \mu_d \neq 0$, we would reject $H_0$ when the following is true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} < t_{n-1, \alpha/2} \quad \text{ or } \quad \frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} > t_{n-1, 1-\alpha/2}
$$

More succinctly, we can reject $H_0$ when $\left|\frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} \right| > t_{n-1, 1-\alpha/2}$
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean Difference (Left-Tailed)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 28.2"}
Let $(X_{i1}, X_{i2})$ for $i = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ be a sequence of independent pairs of normally distributed random variables, (i.e., $\text{Cov}[X_{i1}, X_{i2}] = \sigma_{12}$), with means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and standard deviations $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$. Let $D_i = X_{i1}-X_{i2}$ be independent differences for each pair with mean $\mu_d = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ and standard deviation $\sigma_d = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\sigma_{12}}$

When performing a hypothesis test to test $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ vs $H_A: \mu_d < 0$, we would reject $H_0$ when the following is true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} < t_{n-1,\alpha}
$$
:::

## Hypothesis Test for Population Mean (Right-Tailed, Unknown Variance)

::: {.callout title="Theorem 28.3"}
Let $(X_{i1}, X_{i2})$ for $i = 1, 2, 3, \dots, n$ be a sequence of independent pairs of normally distributed random variables, (i.e., $\text{Cov}[X_{i1}, X_{i2}] = \sigma_{12}$), with means $\mu_1, \mu_2$ and standard deviations $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$. Let $D_i = X_{i1}-X_{i2}$ be independent differences for each pair with mean $\mu_d = \mu_1 - \mu_2$ and standard deviation $\sigma_d = \sqrt{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\sigma_{12}}$

When performing a hypothesis test to test $H_0: \mu_d = 0$ vs $H_A: \mu_d > 0$, we would reject $H_0$ when the following is true:

$$
\frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} > t_{n-1,1-\alpha}
$$
:::

## P-Value for Population Mean Difference (Two-Tailed)

For a two-tailed test involving the population mean difference ($H_A: \mu_d \neq 0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_d}{S_d/\sqrt{n}} \geq \left|\frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} \right| \Bigg| \mu_d = 0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Mean Difference (Left-Tailed)

For a left-tailed test involving the population mean difference ($H_A: \mu_d < 0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_d}{S_d/\sqrt{n}} \leq \frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu_d = 0\right)
$$

## P-Value for Population Mean Difference (Right-Tailed)

For a left-tailed test involving the population mean difference ($H_A: \mu_d > 0$), the p-value would be computed as follows:

$$
P\left(\frac{\bar{X}_d}{S_d/\sqrt{n}} \geq \frac{\bar{x}_d}{s_d/\sqrt{n}} \Bigg| \mu_d = 0\right)
$$

## Ex: Manufacturing

::: {.callout title="Example 28.1"}
An engineering team is investigating whether a new manufacturing process reduces the average weight of metal components produced in a factory. They collect a random sample of 40 batches of raw material and divide each batch in two. They test one half of each batch under the old process and the other under the new process and record the difference in the weights (new minus old). The find that the mean difference for the sample is -1 grams and the sample standard deviation is 3 grams. Perform a hypothesis test to test this hypothesis at the 5% significance level.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_d <- -1
s_d <- 3
n <- 40
t_statistic <- xbar_d/(s_d/sqrt(n))
alpha <- 0.05

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(alpha, n-1), ", P-Value:", pt(t_statistic, n-1))
```

## Ex: Running

::: {.callout title="Example 28.2"}
A sports scientist is studying whether a new running shoe design affects the average running speed of athletes. To test this, the scientist selects a random sample of 35 runners and measures their speed on a treadmill while wearing the old and new shoes. The average speed for each runner is recorded, and the difference in their speeds (new shoe speed minus old shoe speed) is calculated. The mean difference for the sample is found to be 0.5 meters per second with a sample standard deviation of 0.8 meters per second. Perform a hypothesis test at the 1% significance to test this hypothesis.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_d <- 0.5
s_d <- 0.8
n <- 35
t_statistic <- xbar_d/(s_d/sqrt(n))
alpha <- 0.01

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(1-alpha/2, n-1), ", P-Value:", 2*pt(-abs(t_statistic), n-1))
```

## Ex: Solar

::: {.callout title="Example 28.3"}
A renewable energy company is testing whether a new type of solar panel improves energy efficiency compared to traditional panels. They select a random sample of 30 solar panel installations, measuring the energy output of the panels under both the old and new designs over a 30-day period. The difference in energy output (new panel output minus old panel output) is recorded for each installation. The mean difference for the sample is 15 kilowatt-hours with a sample standard deviation of 40 kilowatt-hours. Perform a hypothesis test at the 10% significance level to test this hypothesis.
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
xbar_d <- 15
s_d <- 40
n <- 30
t_statistic <- xbar_d/(s_d/sqrt(n))
alpha <- 0.1

cat("Test Statistic:", t_statistic, ", Critical Value:", qt(1-alpha, n-1), ", P-Value:", 1-pt(t_statistic, n-1))
```

## Ex: Software

::: {.callout title="Example 28.4"}
A software engineering team is investigating whether a new version of their software leads to fewer crashes compared to the previous version. They select a random sample of 50 users and have each user first use the previous version and then use the new version for a period of time and they record the number of crashes they experience with each version. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to test the hypothesis of interest.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
old_vers <- c(12, 8, 11, 9, 11, 9, 12, 11, 11, 11, 10, 12, 6, 11, 12, 13, 12, 10, 11,
         11, 12, 10, 10, 11, 13, 9, 10, 8, 11, 13, 11, 10, 9, 9, 6, 10, 13, 10, 
         12, 11, 11, 12, 10, 10, 11, 9, 9, 13, 9, 8)
new_vers <- c(10, 13, 9, 12, 10, 14, 9, 9, 10, 9, 9, 8, 5, 11, 11, 8, 11, 8, 4, 8, 11,
         10, 9, 12, 8, 9, 11, 10, 8, 12, 10, 9, 7, 10, 10, 11, 9, 7, 10, 9, 8, 9,
         9, 10, 10, 7, 12, 9, 10, 8)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(new_vers, old_vers, alternative = "less", paired = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)$p.value
t.test(old_vers, new_vers, alternative = "greater", paired = TRUE, conf.level = 0.95)$p.value
```

## Ex: Intelligence

::: {.callout title="Example 28.5"}
A psychometrician is studying whether a new version of an intelligence test results in a different average score compared to the previous version. They select a random sample of 30 individuals and have each person take both the old and new versions of the test. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test at the 5% significance level to test the hypothesis of interest.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
new_test <- c(82, 74, 81, 81, 83, 76, 80, 77, 81, 80, 79, 81, 77, 86, 80, 77, 78, 
              80, 80, 78, 79, 78, 80, 74, 76, 81, 81, 82, 86, 81)
old_test <- c(84, 81, 82, 77, 81, 81, 75, 83, 82, 78, 79, 76, 82, 80, 78, 82, 81, 
              79, 82, 83, 79, 81, 82, 77, 80, 80, 78, 78, 81, 82)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(new_test, old_test, paired = TRUE, alternative = "two.sided", conf.level = 0.95)$p.value
```

## Ex: Marketing

::: {.callout title="Example 28.6"}
A company is testing whether a new marketing campaign leads to an increase in average sales (in thousands of dollars). They select a random sample of 40 stores and measure their sales before and after the campaign. Use the data below to perform a hypothesis test at the 1% significance level to test the hypothesis of interest.

```{r, echo = TRUE}
before_camp <- c(51, 49, 53, 49, 52, 49, 52, 50, 48, 51, 50, 52, 50, 50, 48, 49,
                 50, 52, 46, 47, 50, 49, 57, 52, 49, 49, 48, 55, 50, 49, 46, 52,
                 45, 50, 52, 52, 49, 51, 50, 51)
after_camp <- c(54, 48, 48, 51, 49, 52, 45, 51, 50, 56, 52, 50, 51, 51, 53, 48, 
                48, 53, 52, 55, 52, 49, 50, 54, 50, 53, 51, 53, 54, 47, 54, 56, 
                53, 50, 48, 53, 55, 53, 53, 54)
```
:::

. . .

```{r, echo = TRUE}
t.test(after_camp, before_camp, alternative = "greater", paired = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)$p.value
t.test(before_camp, after_camp, alternative = "less", paired = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)$p.value
```
